questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I knew I wanted to go to the US since I've visited before and liked it a lot. The reputation of the university and which schools I had heard of beforehand definitely had its influence on which universities I ended up applying for as well. The US have a lot of schools with a good reputation within my field of study which also contributed to me applying for BU. For me, sports and school spirit also had a certain say when deciding between the universities available in the US. I wanted to experience the atmosphere when going to American football games or other sports games - although Boston University does not have a football team, they still have a lot of other sports teams where you can get this experience, especially ice hockey is popular. Also, I did not realize this before going to Boston, but the city has a lot of other colleges that have, for example, football teams, and you can buy tickets for their games so it ended up working out very well in the end! What courses the universities offered was also an aspect I was very aware of.
When trying to decide which universities I wanted to apply for I also read reports from other UCPH students who went there previously and noted down pros and cons. Things such as a Boston being mentioned as a great city, BU having a cohesive campus, people being friendly and welcoming, there being a lot of different clubs, and great dining halls weighed in a very positive direction.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: What made me rate my overall study experience an 8 instead of 10 was the fact that Boston University did not really seem to do anything to introduce exchange students to each other. It would have been great if some events for exchange students had been held so that we could get to know other people. Other Danish students from UCPH and CBS very quickly became my social circle which was great, but it would have been good to get to know other exchange students. I am not sure if COVID and not being able to gather a lot of people at the same time and place had something to do with it, but if that was the case, then it would have been great if something like the UCPH SCIENCE Buddy Programme had been put in place such that we had had the opportunity to get to know just a small group of other exchange students as well as have some BU students to turn to with any questions we might have had.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy in my opinion. They had a pre-departure website with a lot of important and useful information about course registration, housing, dining plans, visa, and what to bring or buy in Boston. If I had any questions that I could not seem to find the answer for, the BU program coordinator was very helpful!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We did not really receive any assistance when arriving. It should be mentioned that my friend and I went to New York for a week before going to Boston, but we did not get any information about any assistance that we could have gotten. On the pre-departure page, we were informed how to get from, for instance, the airport to the BU campus and what to do when arriving at the campus for check-in at the dorm.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Dorms, suite-style dorms, and apartment style dorms.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
The dorm rooms and suites do not have a kitchen, so you need a dining plan when living in either of these.
You can choose between a variety of different meal plans. Some have a specific amount of meals per semester, some have a number of meals per week, and one is unlimited, i.e., you can go to the dining halls as much as you want. NB: When you swipe yourself into the dining hall, you have used one of your meals. Just be aware of that so you don't accidentally use a meal without intending too.
The apartment style had a kitchen, and you could choose to get a dining plan with a couple of meals a week or something like that.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
It is very expensive! I paid approx. 9000 DKK for a shared room in a dorm with a common bathroom. The showers were, of course, shared as well - fortunately, they are closed off, but remember to bring or buy something to have/carry your shower stuff in.
The floors are usually only boys or girls, and the dorms, at least the one I lived in, at BU are fairly old. Most do not have air-conditioning so be prepared for a hot summer/early Fall if you go for the Fall semester. Also, although the bathrooms are cleaned often, they are still old and not the nicest.
When/if you are applying for on-campus housing, you should consider what you are most comfortable with. If you choose dorm-style, be ready to share a room with a (most likely) 18-20 year old student, and be ready to make compromises if any situations should arise.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Make sure to register for all the sections that constitute your class! Some classes have lectures and discussion, some have lectures and lab, etc. When you register you have to register for all of these individually, so make sure to take note whether you have all the required course sections.
I also made sure to register for more than the 12 credits required for full time student status. At BU and most other US universities, they have a 2 week add/drop period at the beginning of the semester which makes it possible for you to "shop" for classes. Try them out, go to a lecture and so on, and see if you like the class or not.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process was a little confusing in the beginning but as you take the time to roam around on StudentLink, BU's "KUnet", it gets easier. The pre-departure page has the process drawn out, so when the time comes if you follow the information there you are good to go!
When you are looking on the course catalog website, or looking at courses on the different colleges websites, make sure that the course is available during the semester you attend. Some courses are only offered during the Fall or Spring semester. I would it somewhat difficult to find this information up until shortly before registration, so have an open mind when it comes to courses you'd like to take.
If you have your BU login before registration starts, you are able to search the courses you want and add them to your planner. This way, you are able to make your own schedule, and can use the "Graph" option to show your schedule. If you've added all your desired classes to your planner, you can then choose the register for all the classes added to your planner when registration opens! You can also simply search for a specific class and register for it.
NB: for some classes you have to send in a registration form to the BU program coordinator. Also, some classes might be full when you get to register. Sometimes you can find information on how to get on a waitlist on StudentLink. If you cannot seem to find this, try to email the BU program coordinator and ask, if she knows the procedure.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Mainly the pre-departure page, but if I had any questions that I could not find the answer for, the BU program coordinator was more than happy to answer my questions through email.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful. I had one class I really wanted to take but it was full when our registration started. I got on the waitlist but unfortunately never got off of it. This class, however, had lectures simultaneously with another class I also wanted which I ended up getting into, so I decided to go with the one I got into. Thus, in general, I'd say my registration was easy and successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
1. If you have your BU login, register as soon as possible, or get on waitlist for the class as soon as possible. Classes tend to fill up quick, in my experience.
2. Make sure you have registered for all the required class sections.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took a 300- and two 500-level classes. The 300-level courses are described as Advanced undergraduate, and the 500-level courses are described as Advanced undergraduate and/or graduate courses. Personally, I think these course levels, and the combination I ended up with, was fitting for me. The courses definitely required a fair amount of work on my part, but I also tend to spend a lot of time on the different aspects of the classes, so the fact that I spent a lot of time should not steer you way from taking classes on these levels.
A fair amount of the concepts that were presented in the two genetics classes has been presented in previous courses at UCPH, however, I do think I learned a lot - many new concepts and new knowledge about different model organisms, and the concepts we had heard of before were developed further.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was/is very different. Your final grade consists of a lot of different components - not just a final exam as many of the courses we have encountered. Participation, written assignments, and approximately two midterms/exams and a final exam are things taken into consideration for the final grade. If you are between two grades, the professor might bump you up if you've attended the classes in-person (we were able to follow two of my classes online if you got COVID, or didn't feel comfortable coming in for lectures), had attended office hours during the semester, or in other ways expressed curiosity for the course topics.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: CAS BI 311. General Microbiology, CAS BI 513. Genetics Laboratory, and BI572. Advanced Genetics.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all the courses I took for future exchange students.
If you find viruses interesting, then the last part of the General Microbiology course is definitely for you. I found that section especially interesting. Additionally, I just started my bachelor's project, and a couple of things presented in the lab section of General Microbiology have already been mentioned. I think the time I spent on the course will turn out to be well spent since I learned a lot of basic information about microbiological organisms which can be used in the future.
Advanced Genetics is a really good course if you want to learn about genetics in other organisms as well as in humans. We have a pretty good grasp on the human section of the cause because of Medical Genetics, however, Drosophila and C. elegans genetics are also presented which I think will be very helpful when reading scientific literature in the future and to know in general. A very thorough run-down of knock-outs in mice, as well as deciding what methods to use to investigate specific things is also one of the aspects in the class that I found very useful!
Genetics Laboratory was a great course to get some hands-on experience (especially since we unfortunately had our Protein chemistry and Enzymology II course online and not in-person). We also got to do a lot of PCR preparation and sequence analysis on mutations in the two designated genes we worked with. In general, I think this course was very giving, although it was a little unstructured.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you want to go to sports games you either have to buy a SportsPass (130 USD, lasts the entire year), or you have to buy tickets for every game you attend (approx. 20 USD every time). I decided to purchase the Sports Pass since I wanted to go to a lot of ice hockey games - but it should be mentioned that I got a free hockey jersey since I went to 8 Men's Ice Hockey home games.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Printing was less expensive - we got the first approx. 100 black and white pages for free (i.e., you got 8 USD to print for, and a double sided black and white printed piece of paper was very cheap).
My phone plan was also less expensive than expected. I ended up getting a World Plan through CBB where I could send texts and call people in Denmark and the US for free, and I could use the data included. I was told I would only be able to use the plan for 2-3 months before I would be contacted somehow and told to "change my behavior", i.e., "go back to Denmark". I never got a text or email telling me to change anything and just kept using it. No additional charges came either. I even spent some time after my semester ended with some family in the US and did not arrive back in Denmark until January, and my plan still worked. So I definitely saved a little bit of money since I know my friend got a T Mobile plan in the US where she paid 40 USD each month (plus a 10 USD fee when she registered and got her number).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
They have all sorts of clubs for students at BU - athletic, cultural, academic, social etc. Right before the beginning of the Fall semester they had a giant fair-kind-of-thing where all the clubs had a table where you could go and chat with some of the members of that team/club and sign up if you wanted to.
I personally didn't participate in any BU related clubs, but I joined a Team Handball Team in Boston consisting of a lot of people from all around the world, which was a lot of fun!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
In regard to cultural activities, besides the cultural clubs you might be able to join, BU also planned events such as Pumpkin Decoration around Halloween, and probably a lot more that I just don't remember.
In relation to athletic activities, you were able to join different sports teams. Some of the competitive teams have try-outs, whereas others you can pretty much just join. They also have intramural sports clubs where you play others - students or faculty - within BU. The school also has FitRec - the Fitness and Recreation Center - where you can use the gym and swimming pools for free.
Different social activities were also available. Before the semester started, they had a lot of different events as part of "Weeks of Welcome", and different social and/or cultural events also took place throughout the semester.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a club or sports team - whether it is associated to BU or not. I found it really nice to be able to stay physically active through practices with my handball team, and you get to meet a lot of people and make new friends and acquaintances. It is also a great way to get a more diverse way of living such that school isn't the only thing. Sometimes you also get to travel the country or the nearby states or cities with your team or club which is really cool!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Of course, experience Boston. Walk the Freedom Trail, go to museums, walk up and down Newbury Street, go to Boston Common and the Public Garden. Definitely have a study day at Boston Public Library, and go hiking in Blue Hills if you enjoy that. Visit Harvard University and MIT, experience Cambridge, watch a movie at Regal Fenway movie theater. You should also try to go to a Red Sox game at Fenway Park, watch some american football at some of the other universities in Boston (e.g., MIT, Harvard, or Boston College), and catch a BU Men's hockey game. You can also take the T to Providence or Salem, maybe rent a car to go to Cape Cod, or take the train to New York City for a couple of days.
Boston and the surrounding area has a lot to offer so you won't find yourself bored!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy for me, I would say. I've been to the US a couple of times before, although that was in the South, but I had a pretty good understanding of the American culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Try to join a club or team at BU.
If you are in a smaller class or lab, try to hit up a conversation with some of the other students there.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't really find any cultural differences challenging - mostly interesting and funny (such as the fact that they call what I would say is a Chicken Burger a Chicken Sandwich).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciate the open-mindedness of talking to strangers out in public - although, people in Boston are more reserved compared to people in the South. One of my first days at BU, I was done getting the required vaccine shots. I was waiting for the T, and it started raining a little. Two girls, each with an umbrella walked by, but then one of them ended up asking if I wanted to share hers. We then started talking a little, and ended up chatting on the T until they got of.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Try to take initiative to talk to people - other international/exchange students, and Americans. From what I've experienced, BU does not really seem to initiate any social gatherings between any of the international students (one of the exchange students had to suggest making a WhatsApp group for all the exchange students at BU).
2. Be prepared for a very different way of "doing school" - there will most likely be a couple of assignments, and at least two midterms/exams and one final exam.
3. Don't be stressed about wanting to see all of Boston in the beginning - although time passes by fast, you have plenty of time and weekends to see and experience what you want!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
1. If you have the time and energy, try to apply for some scholarships from private companies and foundations. It is very expensive to attend BU - mostly because of the housing cost.
2. Make sure to start your visa application right when you receive the documents from BU. You can even start before getting them - you don't really need the information from BU until the last part of the DS-160 form (the first form you have to complete, if I remember correctly). It was really difficult for me and other Danish exchange students to get our visas because of the COVID situation, but I have heard it is somewhat difficult to get appointments at the US Embassy even when things are normal.
3. I would recommend taking the TOEFL test in person, if possible. I did it at home, and it was kind of a hassle since you had to clear your entire desk, you had to show the proctor your entire room, and sudden movements can be interpreted as cheating even if you are not. In general, there were just a lot of preparation to do besides just preparing for the test itself.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to experience the culture of Boston and the East cost of the US. Meeting other Danish exchange students, people from all around the world, and making great connections.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Before the exchange, it was getting our visa. However, during my exchange, it was getting to know exchange students from other countries. I ended up socializing primarily with other Danish exchange students at BU, a couple of American students from my classes, and my handball teammates, but meeting other exchange students would have made my experience even better than it already is.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
